I01: 0/2
- Criterion 1: not met. The fact is about initial Spanish ability, but it runs the wrong way: streak holders starting as beginners while the other group had already studied Spanish would make the later score gap more, not less, attributable to the streaks.
- Criterion 2: not met. The explanation treats any starting difference as unfair, but this difference does not make it more plausible that the later gap was already there before the streaks.
- Tip: A weakener about starting ability has to put the eventual streak holders ahead at sign-up, or at least no further behind than they were later.
I02: 2/2
- Criterion 1: met. “The letter is written on Holt paper” is an unstated bridge that lets Holt’s 1801 mark date this sheet, not a restated premise or the conclusion.
- Criterion 2: met. It is no stronger than needed: if this sheet was not Holt paper, Holt’s start date would not set a lower bound for it.
- Tip: Keep necessary assumptions tied to this sheet, as you did, rather than to every papermaker who ever used a hare mark.
I03: 1/1
- Criterion 1: met. The sentence states the author’s recommendation that the society should not oppose converting the silo into apartments, not the intermediate preservation claim or the members’ view.
- Tip: When a passage opens with the recommendation, that opening claim is usually the main conclusion even if a later sentence sounds conclusive.
I04: 0/2
- Criterion 1: not met. The ad concludes that streaks made learners better speakers; the answer says the ad assumes the reverse, so it does not correctly tie the error to this inference.
- Criterion 2: not met. It then endorses the ad’s causal claim instead of naming an explanation the argument leaves open, such as better speakers finding streaks easier to keep.
- Tip: State the author’s actual inference first, then name a rival explanation the premises do not rule out.
